idiom_name: tokio runtime with AsyncRead/AsyncWrite and the epoll/kqueue/IOCP I/O driver
implementation_notes: async/await is language syntax: an async function compiles to a Future that returns Pending and is woken through its Waker when the awaited operation completes. The standard library ships the traits but no executor, so tokio supplies the task scheduler and an I/O driver backed by the operating system event queue (epoll, kqueue, IOCP), which observes completions and wakes the tasks; handlers are the code after await and spawn_blocking covers work that cannot be made asynchronous.
pitfalls: Dropping a future cancels it: a spawned task can be cancelled at any await point, so cleanup must be explicit.
A blocking call inside an async task stalls a scheduler worker; blocking file, DNS or FFI work belongs in spawn_blocking.
Holding a std::sync::Mutex guard across .await is a deadlock risk; use tokio::sync::Mutex or scope the guard.

variants.name: io_uring driver (tokio-uring)
variants.implementation_notes: tokio-uring replaces the readiness-based driver with an io_uring driver: operations are submitted to the kernel submission queue and the buffer is passed by ownership, returning together with the completion queue event, which is the pattern's true completion semantics rather than futures layered over readiness. The trade is a Linux-only, recent-kernel requirement and an ownership style that differs from ordinary &mut slice reads.
pitfalls: Requires Linux with a recent kernel; the crate's README documents kernels even as recent as 5.4 as unsupported.
Buffers move into the operation and come back with the completion, so code that expects to reuse the buffer after submission will not compile - by design.
The crate is young and its API surface is narrower than tokio's.
